rv.q: Hodge is the primary reason this riotously funny and, yes, emotionally affecting revival of the Jerry Herman-Harvey Fierstein musical has returned to Broadway only five years after its last New York appearance.
Their big, glitzy musical comedy hit of 1983 turns out to have a tender heart.

Terry Johnson’s inspired revival of Jerry Herman and Harvey Fierstein’s musical, starring a happily mismatched Kelsey Grammer and Douglas Hodge (in a bravura Broadway debut), delivers the unexpected lesson that in theater, shabby can be not just chic but redemptive.
Harvey Fierstein's book, which celebrates nonconformity and generosity, still resonates, while Herman's songs are downright unsinkable.

Terry Johnson's London staging and its Olivier Award-winning star, Douglas Hodge, inject this 1983. Jerry Herman-Harvey Fierstein musical with ingenious razzmatazz and a heartbreaking humanity that its immediate predecessor lacked.
By the end of this well-paced production, it's hard not to concur with the refrain of Albin's second-act number: The best of times is now.
Now La Cage is a New York treat worth savoring.
The human-scale production focuses on the laughs and deeper emotions instead of trying to wow you with extravagance.
Hodge and Grammer, who sings, dances and is both charming and humorous, have an admirable rapport, and persuasively suggest the long-term affection between Georges and Albin.
They all seem to be having a swell time, as will you — so long as you can keep up with them.
Their latest import is "La Cage aux Folles," which opened Sunday at the Longacre Theatre and showcases a delightful turn by British actor Douglas Hodge as a motherly drag star.

cn.t: This scaled-down revival wins critics over with Douglas Hodge's exuberant, Olivier-winning performance as Albin and Terry Johnson's heartfelt direction, proving the show merited another Broadway run despite arriving just five years after its last revival.

vs.sum: The Longacre Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions, even from the balcony, and the sound quality is consistently praised. While the seating is a bit narrow, it provides average comfort for most patrons. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant Beaux Arts interior, and facilities are typical for a Broadway venue, with some lines at intermission but generally manageable.

acc.note: Small restroom-only elevator (may not accommodate all wheelchairs). 3 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra.
